house-gop-218-jan-2027.base_rate:
The president's party has lost House seats in most midterms since WWII (about 18 of 20).
Losses were 40 or more seats in 2018 (-41), 2010 (-63) and 2006 (-30).
A Republican net loss of 3 or more would drop them below 218, and the current Republican count is already near 217-220.

house-gop-218-jan-2027.text:
The nonpartisan election handicapper the Cook Political Report moved 18 House race ratings toward Democrats on Friday, October 9, 2026, less than four weeks before the November 3, 2026 midterm elections.
The shifts push Cook’s projected outcome to a Democratic net gain of nine to 19 seats, which would give the party between 224 and 234 seats — comfortably above the 218 needed for a majority.
◉ Key Facts
- ►Cook moved 18 House race ratings toward Democrats on Friday, October 9, 2026, roughly 25 days before the November 3, 2026 midterms.
- ►Cook now projects a Democratic net gain of nine to 19 seats, putting the party’s likely House total between 224 and 234 seats — above the 218 needed for control.
- ►Nine Republican incumbents saw their races shift toward Democrats, including Reps.
Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Zach Nunn of Iowa, Ryan Mackenzie, Scott Perry and Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, Bill Huizenga of Michigan, Rob Wittman of Virginia, French Hill of Arkansas and Victoria Spartz of Indiana.
- ►Five Democratic incumbents — Reps.
Susie Lee (Nev.), Tom Suozzi and Laura Gillen (N.Y.), Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (Wash.) and Don Davis (N.C.) — saw their races tighten further in Democrats’ favor, along with four open seats in Nebraska’s 2nd, Iowa’s 2nd, Kentucky’s 6th and Maine’s 2nd districts.
- ►Cook House editor Erin Covey wrote that Democrats now need to win only about 20% of the Toss Up races to reach a majority, assuming the seats that favor Democrats in Cook’s ratings all break their way.
The Cook Political Report, widely regarded as one of the most closely watched nonpartisan election forecasters in Washington, cited mounting headwinds for Republican candidates tied to the ongoing conflict involving Iran, rising energy prices and broader economic uncertainty.
Cook’s U.S.
House of Representatives editor Erin Covey wrote in her analysis, “With these new moves, we’re also adjusting our range: the most likely outcome is now that Democrats will pick up nine to 19 seats,” adding that “At this point, Democrats only need to win 20 percent of the Toss Ups to get to a majority, assuming the seats that favor Democrats in our ratings all break their way.” Of the races Cook currently classifies as toss-ups, Cook currently labels 21 House contests as “Toss Up,” including 15 Republican-held seats and six Democrat-held districts.
That imbalance means Republicans are defending far more of the most competitive turf than Democrats are, a structural disadvantage that becomes more consequential the longer unfavorable political conditions persist.
The ratings shift arrives despite an aggressive Republican effort to blunt Democratic momentum through advertising.
According to reporting on the shift, Cook Political’s Erin Covey wrote that “In the final weeks of the election, Republicans have hoped that a massive ad campaign effort could dent Democratic candidates’ images and shore up Republicans struggling to free themselves of the anchor of President Donald Trump,” but “With less than four weeks to go, that heavy spending has yet to move the needle.” The scale of the broader shift across forecasters has also drawn attention: according to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, just since Labor Day, Cook Political, Inside Elections, Sabato’s Crystal Ball, and Fox News have made 101 rating changes in Democrats’ favor.
Republicans have pushed back on the characterization that the race is slipping away.
NRCC spokesman Mike Marinella said in a statement that “House races are won in the districts, one by one, with battle-tested candidates and messages that work,” adding that “Pundits in D.C.
can keep guessing, but voters on the ground have a clear contrast between common sense and crazy,” and predicting that “in November, we’re going to win.”
| Category | Districts/Races |
|---|---|
| GOP incumbents shifted toward Democrats | Miller-Meeks & Nunn (Iowa), Mackenzie, Perry & Fitzpatrick (Pa.), Huizenga (Mich.), Wittman (Va.), Hill (Ark.), Spartz (Ind.) |
| Democratic incumbents strengthened | Lee (Nev.), Suozzi & Gillen (N.Y.), Gluesenkamp Perez (Wash.), Davis (N.C.) |
| Open seats shifted toward Democrats | Nebraska’s 2nd, Iowa’s 2nd, Kentucky’s 6th, Maine’s 2nd |
| New projected House outcome | Democrats: 224-234 seats (net gain of 9-19) |
📚 Background & Context
The Cook Political Report is one of several nonpartisan handicappers, alongside Inside Elections and Sabato’s Crystal Ball, that political strategists, donors and journalists use to gauge the competitiveness of individual House, Senate and gubernatorial races.
The party that does not control the White House has historically gained House seats in midterm elections in most cycles since World War II, a pattern rooted in lower turnout among the president’s supporters and backlash against the incumbent administration’s record.
Rating changes are forecasts based on polling, fundraising, candidate quality and political environment — not predictions of certain outcomes, and Cook and other handicappers routinely revise their ratings again before Election Day as new data emerges.
With roughly three and a half weeks remaining until the November 3, 2026 midterms, both parties are expected to pour additional resources into the newly competitive districts, and further ratings movement from Cook and rival forecasters is likely as early voting begins and more polling is released.
The ultimate test of these projections will come when votes are counted on Election Day, when the accuracy of this cycle’s forecasting models — and the political environment they are attempting to capture — will be fully revealed.
💬 What People Are Saying
Based on public reaction across social media and news platforms, here is the general consensus on this story:
- 🔴Republican voices argue the ratings reflect Washington punditry rather than conditions on the ground, with GOP operatives insisting local candidates and messaging will carry races that national forecasters are writing off prematurely.
- 🔵Democratic strategists and committees are pointing to the shift as validation of a building wave, citing voter anger over the economy and the ongoing Iran conflict as evidence the party is positioned to retake the House majority.
- 🟠Political observers across the spectrum note that while the ratings shift is a meaningful signal, it remains a projection rather than a result, and both parties are bracing for a volatile final stretch before the November 3, 2026 election.
Note: Social reactions represent general public sentiment and do not reflect Political.org’s editorial position.

house-gop-218-jan-2027.text:
On April 21, 2026, Rep.
Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick (D-Fla.) resigned, leaving Florida's 20th Congressional District vacant.
Cherfilus-McCormick’s resignation came after the U.S.
House of Representatives Ethics Committee announced on March 27 that it had determined that she violated the chamber’s campaign finance rules, finding that she had misappropriated disaster relief funds for campaign purposes.
A hearing was scheduled for April 21 to discuss possible sanctions.
As of April 21, 2026, Republicans have a 217 to 213 majority in the U.S.
House, with four vacancies.
Additionally, Rep.
Kevin Kiley (I-Calif.) is an independent who caucuses with Republicans.
Cherfilus-McCormick’s electoral history
In 2022, Cherfilus-McCormick ran for the U.S.
House in Florida’s 20th Congressional District, after then-incumbent Rep.
Alcee Hastings (D-Fla.) died.
In the special general election, Cherfilus-McCormick defeated Jason Mariner (R) 79% to 19.4%.
Cherfilus-McCormick won re-election in the 2022 regular general election by 44.6 percentage points.
In the 2024 general election, she ran unopposed.
Vacancies in the 119th Congress
So far in the 119th Congress, there have been 12 in the U.S.
House and four in the U.S.
Senate.
Of those vacancies:
- Three in the U.S.
Senate were filled via appointment.
- One in the U.S.
Senate was filled when Sen.
Jim Justice (R-W.Va.) was sworn into office 11 days after the start of the 119th Congress.
Justice delayed his swearing-in in order to fulfill the remainder of his term as governor of West Virginia.
- Eight in the U.S.
House were filled after special election winners were sworn in.
As of April 21, 2026, the vacancies in Florida's 20th Congressional District, California's 1st Congressional District, California's 14th Congressional District, and Texas' 23rd Congressional District have not been filled.
Of the 16 vacancies, the longest was in Texas' 18th Congressional District, which became vacant on March 5, 2025, following the death of Rep.
Sylvester Turner (D-Texas).
The vacancy ended on Feb.
2, 2026, after 334 days.
Congressional vacancies since the 113th Congress
During the 113th through 118th Congresses, there were 88 vacancies in the U.S.
House and 16 in the U.S.
Senate.
The average length of a vacancy in the U.S.
Senate during that period was seven days.
The average length of a vacancy in the U.S.
House during that period was 138 days.
The longest vacancy in the U.S.
Senate during that period was in New Jersey.
The vacancy occurred during the 118th Congress, when Sen.
Bob Menendez (D-N.J.) resigned on Aug.
20, 2024.
Following Menendez's resignation, the seat was vacant for 20 days.
The longest vacancy in the U.S.
House during that period was in Michigan's 13th Congressional District.
The vacancy occurred during the 115th Congress, when Rep.
John Conyers, Jr.
(D-Mich.) resigned on Dec.
5, 2017.
Following Conyers' resignation, the seat was vacant for 359 days.
